An adze is a hand-held cutting tool used for shaping, smoothing, or hollowing out wood. Think of it as a close cousin of the axe — but with one important difference that changes everything about how it works.

An adze has two parts: a handle and a blade.

The blade is attached to the handle, but here's the key: unlike an axe (where the blade faces away from you, like a wedge you drive forward), the blade of an adze is set at a right angle to the handle — meaning the sharp edge faces toward the user and curves slightly downward, like the blade of a hoe or a garden mattock. If you hold the handle horizontally in front of you, the blade would be pointing down at the ground.

The user swings the adze in a controlled, scooping or chipping motion — downward and toward themselves — to shave or chip off layers of wood. The curved blade allows it to bite into a surface and peel away wood smoothly rather than splitting it.

Imagine a sculptor chipping away at a block of marble, but here, the material is wood and the tool is the adze. Each swing removes a small sliver or chip. Over many strokes, an uneven, rough surface becomes flat and clean, or a solid piece of wood becomes hollowed out.

1. Hand adze — Has a short handle, roughly the length of your forearm. The user kneels or crouches over the piece of wood and uses precise, controlled strokes. This is better for detail work and fine smoothing.

2. Foot adze (or long-handled adze) — Has a long handle like an axe. The user stands over a log on the ground and swings the tool down between their feet in a steady rhythm. This is used for heavy work like squaring off a large timber log.

The adze is a tool of the woodworker and the carpenter, and its jobs include:

  • Squaring a log — turning a rough, round log into a flat-sided beam for construction.
  • Hollowing out wood — carving the inside of a wooden canoe, bowl, or trough.
  • Smoothing a surface — evening out rough or uneven planks before finishing.
  • Shaping curved forms — creating concave surfaces that a flat plane cannot easily reach.

Before machines existed, shipbuilders used adzes constantly to shape the curved wooden hulls of boats. Timber framers used them to prepare beams for houses and barns. Almost any craft involving large wooden structures depended heavily on the adze.
How It Differs From an Axe

This is the most important distinction to understand clearly:

FeatureAxeAdze

An axe blade runs parallel to the handle — when you swing, the blade drives forward into the wood, splitting it apart along the grain. It's a tool of force and splitting.

An adze blade runs perpendicular to the handle — when you swing, the blade sweeps across the surface of the wood, shaving it. It's a tool of precision and shaping.

In short: an axe splits wood; an adze shapes it.

The adze is an ancient tool — among the oldest known to humans — but it is still used today by:

  • Traditional woodworkers and craftspeople who prefer hand tools.
  • Boat builders working with traditional wooden vessels.
  • Timber framers constructing barns, cabins, and heritage buildings.
  • Wood sculptors and carvers working on large pieces.
  • Indigenous craftspeople around the world, for whom the adze remains a central cultural and practical tool (the adzes used in Pacific Island and Native American traditions, for example, are historically significant).

In industrial or modern construction, the adze has largely been replaced by power planers, routers, and electric chisels — but for anyone working with their hands on wood in a traditional or artistic way, the adze remains an irreplaceable and highly skilled tool.

You might see it used like this:

  • "The shipwright ran his adze along the keel, shaving the beam until it was perfectly smooth."
  • "He hollowed out the canoe with nothing but an adze and weeks of patient work."
  • "The carpenter reached for his adze to flatten the warped surface of the old timber."

If you need one sentence to anchor the word in your mind:

An adze is a curved-bladed woodworking tool swung in a scooping motion to shave and shape wood, looking like an axe but with the blade turned sideways so it cuts across the surface rather than into it.
